newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel tells Czech govt to set long-term policy.
newsitem.headline: Havel tells Czech govt to set long-term policy.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel said on Wednesday the beleaguered government had to offer a clear picture of the future to regain public confidence and stop living from one emergency package to the next.

Speaking after meetings with the parliamentary leadership of the four strongest parties, he said it was not enough for the reconstructed centre-right cabinet to govern with just the narrow victory it won in a vote of confidence last week.

"It's not enough only to yell fire when something is burning, it's not enough just to pack packages (of emergency measures) and just react on the immediate situation, but it's necessary to be a subject of history and look to the future," Havel told journalists.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's three-party coalition government squeaked through a 101-99 parliamentary vote of confidence last week after shuffling three cabinet seats and announcing its second package of emergency measures in as many months to fix an ailing economy.
The government's popularity has plummeted to about 20 percent in recent opinion polls after the Czech crown dropped sharply in May while economic growth stagnated and the trade gap widened.

After the central bank was forced to give in to speculative pressure and float the Czech crown on May 27, Klaus announced sharp budget cuts, wage freezes and other austerity measures while acknowledging that policy mistakes were made.

Havel said he thought the government would continue to suffer a lack of confidence unless it provided the public "a certain assurance, a certain hope... a certain feeling that the sacrifices which are requested have some sense."

"If it will...string from meeting to meeting, from votes of confidence to votes of no confidence then from package to package, then most possibly it will not do much for strenghtening its trustworthiness," Havel said.

The Czech news agency CTK quoted the leader of Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) in the Senate upper house, Milan Kondr, as telling Havel he was "sceptical that the ODS would take part in another government" should the present one fall.
The three-party coalition, in which the ODS holds half the 16 cabinet seats, has been torn by infighting between the two right-wing parties and the centrist Christian Democrats.
Havel, in answer to a question, said that the constitution had provisions for the possibility of the government falling.

"If this government lost the confidence of parliament and if this government handed in its resignation, then there exists many constitutionally legitimate possibilities how this coalition could govern further, or how a government could govern with the support of the present coalition," he said.
Havel's role is largely ceremonial but he would play a key part in forging a new government if the current one fell.
Some political analysts have said that if the government collapsed, a cabinet of unaffiliated experts might be possible with the support of the current coalition.
